definition: A worked example (steel producer, 1990) illustrating how a correlation-based proxy hedge between two power price zones can fail over a long horizon as the zones' fundamentals diverge.
core_idea: A PJM-East steel producer, lacking exchange-traded futures for its own zone, hedged 25 years of electricity exposure using PJM-West futures because the two zones' prices were highly correlated (both peak on the same hot summer days due to shared weather); over the following decade PJM-East prices rose sharply due to regional population/demand growth while PJM-West prices fell, and because correlation stayed high throughout, no one investigated the diverging price levels until the hedge had accumulated a large loss.
key_points: Setup: PJM-East (near Washington, D.C./Baltimore) had no exchange-traded futures; PJM-West (western MD/WV/PA) did.
The producer bought $500 million notional of PJM-West forwards ($20 million/year for 25 years) after confirming high correlation between the two zones.
Over the next 10 years, Baltimore-Washington population/commercial growth pushed PJM-East prices up, while PJM-West, without similar growth, saw prices decline.
Correlation stayed high the whole time because both zones share weather (peaks on hot summer days) even as absolute price levels diverged.
The day-to-day correlation masked the multi-year trend divergence, so the widening gap went unnoticed until the hedge had produced a large loss.
relationships: Concrete illustration of "Correlated does not mean a good hedge."
trading_implications: Long-dated proxy hedges across locations need periodic review of the actual price/basis trend, not just an initial or ongoing correlation check, since correlation reflects co-movement of swings, not convergence of price levels.
caveats: Assuming that because two zones' prices peak and trough together (weather-driven correlation), the zones' price levels will also stay close together over time.
